transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: A new study has found that drinking coffee in moderation may have several health benefits, including a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain types of cancer, according to researchers at the University of Oxford. The study analyzed data from over 200,000 people and found that those who drank 2 to 3 cups of coffee per day had the lowest risk of various health problems compared to those who didn't drink coffee or who drank more than 5 cups a day. Both regular and decaffeinated coffee showed similar benefits, suggesting that caffeine isn't the only beneficial component—coffee is also rich in antioxidants and other beneficial compounds. Researchers caution that more research is needed, but they say that moderate coffee consumption can be part of a healthy diet for most people.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: The city of San Francisco has become the first major city in the United States to require all new buildings to have solar panels on their roofs, as part of its efforts to combat climate change and increase renewable energy use. The rule applies to all new residential and commercial buildings up to 10 stories tall, and it's estimated that it will add thousands of new solar installations each year. San Francisco already has a goal of getting 100 percent of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030, and this new requirement is an important step toward that goal. Supporters say that the rule will help reduce greenhouse gas emissions, create jobs in the solar industry, and save building owners money on their electricity bills in the long run. Critics argue that the requirement will make new construction more expensive, especially for affordable housing.

paras: Archaeologists in Egypt have discovered the remains of a 2,000-year-old Roman temple in the city of Alexandria, according to a new announcement from the Egyptian Ministry of Antiquities. The discovery includes the remains of the temple's foundations, columns, and walls, as well as various artifacts like statues, pottery, and coins. Archaeologists say that the discovery will help them learn more about the Roman period in Egypt and about the religious practices of the time. Alexandria was one of the most important cities in the ancient world, and this new discovery adds to our understanding of its rich history.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Mark): Hey Lisa, I heard you joined a gym recently. How's it going?
Woman (Lisa): It's going pretty well! I've been going for about a month now, and I'm really starting to get into it.
Man: That's great! What made you decide to join a gym?

Woman: Well, I've been feeling really out of shape lately. I sit at a desk all day for work, and I don't get much exercise. I was starting to feel tired all the time, and I knew I needed to make a change.
Man: Yeah, I know what you mean. It's easy to fall into a sedentary lifestyle when you work an office job. What gym did you join?
Woman: I joined that new gym downtown—FitLife. Have you heard of it?
Man: Yeah, I've heard of it. I've thought about joining too, but I'm not sure if I'd actually go. I'm pretty lazy when it comes to exercise.
Woman: Oh, you should definitely join! It's actually really fun once you get into it. And they have all kinds of classes—yoga, spinning, Zumba, boxing... there's something for everyone.
Man: Classes? I don't know... classes sound intimidating. What if I'm bad at it?
Woman: Oh, don't worry about that! Everyone starts somewhere. The instructors are really good at helping beginners. And no one is judging you—everyone is just focused on their own workout.
Man: Hmm, maybe. What else do they have?
Woman: They have all the usual equipment too—treadmills, ellipticals, weights, machines. And they have a pool and a sauna too.
Man: A pool? That sounds nice. I used to swim a lot when I was younger.
Woman: You should try it! Swimming is great exercise, and it's easy on your joints. They even have lap swim hours every morning and evening.
Man: That's tempting. How much does membership cost?
Woman: It's about $50 a month, which I think is pretty reasonable. And they have a free trial week, so you can try it out before you commit.
Man: A free trial week? That's a good deal. What do I need to bring if I go?
Woman: Just workout clothes, shoes, and a water bottle. They have towels and lockers you can use. And they have showers too, so you can shower after your workout.
Man: That's convenient. Hey, would you want to go together sometime? I'd feel less intimidated if I went with someone.
Woman: Sure! That would be fun. We could go after work one day this week. I usually go on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
Man: How about this Tuesday? I can meet you there after work.
Woman: Perfect! I can show you around and introduce you to some of the classes if you want. Or we could just do our own thing.
Man: Maybe we can start with just the gym equipment and the pool, and then I can try a class later once I'm more comfortable.
Woman: Sounds good to me. And hey, even if you only go once or twice a week, that's better than nothing. You don't have to go every day to see benefits.
Man: Yeah, that's true. Alright, I'm in. Thanks for encouraging me, Lisa.
Woman: No problem! I'm excited to have a workout buddy. Okay, I'll see you Tuesday after work.
Man: See you Tuesday!
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

9. What does Lisa say about group classes?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Sophie): Hey James, I need your help. I'm planning a trip to Japan next month, and I have so many questions.
Man (James): Japan! That's exciting. I've been there twice, so maybe I can help. What do you want to know?
Woman: Well, first of all, I'm a vegetarian. Will I have trouble finding food? I've heard Japanese food is really heavy on fish and meat.

Man: Hmm, that's a good question. It can be a little tricky, especially outside of the big cities. But in Tokyo and Kyoto, there are actually quite a few vegetarian and vegan restaurants these days. And even regular restaurants often have vegetarian options—like tempura vegetables, tofu dishes, rice bowls with vegetables...
Woman: That's a relief. What about ramen? I love ramen, but most ramen broth is made with meat or fish stock, right?

Man: Yeah, most traditional ramen is meat-based. But there are vegetarian ramen places now, especially in the bigger cities. You just have to look for them. And you can always ask for vegetarian options—most places are pretty accommodating if you explain.
Woman: Good to know. What about transportation? What's the best way to get around?

Man: The train system is amazing in Japan, especially in Tokyo. It's super efficient and goes everywhere. You should definitely get a Suica or Pasmo card—it's a rechargeable card you can use on trains, subways, buses, and even at convenience stores.
Woman: What about between cities? I want to go from Tokyo to Kyoto. Should I fly or take the train?

Man: Definitely take the shinkansen—the bullet train. It's fast, comfortable, and really convenient. The trip from Tokyo to Kyoto only takes about 2 and a half hours. And you get to see the countryside along the way. It's worth the experience.
Woman: That sounds great. I've always wanted to ride a bullet train. What about etiquette? Are there things I should know about so I don't accidentally offend anyone?

Man: Oh, good question. There are a few things. First, you should always take off your shoes when you enter someone's home, and also at some traditional restaurants, temples, and shrines. Second, don't eat or drink while walking around—it's considered rude. And third, don't tip—tipping isn't customary in Japan, and it can actually be considered rude.
Woman: Wow, good to know. I would have probably tried to tip and embarrassed myself. What else?

Man: Let's see... when you're on the train, you should keep your voice down and not talk on the phone. And if you go to a temple or shrine, there's usually a purification fountain at the entrance—you're supposed to wash your hands and mouth before entering.
Woman: That's interesting. I'll have to remember that. What about money? Do they accept credit cards everywhere?

Man: Not everywhere, actually. A lot of smaller shops, restaurants, and temples are cash-only. You should make sure to have enough yen with you. Convenience stores usually have ATMs that accept foreign cards, so you can withdraw cash there.
Woman: Okay, good to know. Is there anything else I should know?

Man: Hmm... learn a few basic Japanese phrases. People really appreciate it when you make an effort. "Hello," "thank you," "excuse me," and "sorry" are the most important ones. And don't worry if you don't speak the language well—most people in tourist areas speak at least a little English, and they're very patient.
Woman: Thanks so much, James. You've been so helpful. I feel a lot more prepared now.
Man: No problem! You're going to have an amazing time. Japan is such a unique and wonderful country. Let me know if you have more questions.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The history of chocolate is a long and fascinating story that goes back thousands of years to ancient Mesoamerica. Today, chocolate is one of the most popular foods in the world, enjoyed by billions of people in many different forms. But it wasn't always the sweet, creamy treat we know today.

The story of chocolate begins with the Maya and Aztec civilizations in Central America, who were the first people to grow cacao trees and make chocolate. But their chocolate was very different from ours—it was a bitter, spicy drink made from ground cacao beans mixed with water, chili peppers, and other spices. It wasn't sweet at all. The Maya and Aztecs used chocolate in religious ceremonies, as medicine, and even as currency. Cacao beans were so valuable that they were used as money.

Chocolate was brought to Europe by Spanish explorers in the 16th century. The Spanish added sugar and cinnamon to make it sweeter, and it became a popular drink among the wealthy and aristocracy. But chocolate was still very expensive, and only the rich could afford it.

In the 19th century, the invention of new technologies made it possible to mass-produce chocolate, which made it cheaper and more accessible to everyone. The invention of the cocoa press made it possible to separate cocoa butter from cocoa powder, and the invention of conching made chocolate smoother and creamier. This is when chocolate started to become the sweet, solid treat we know today.

Companies like Cadbury in England and Nestlé in Switzerland started producing chocolate on a large scale, and chocolate became a popular food for people of all classes. Milk chocolate was invented, which was even sweeter and creamier than dark chocolate.

In the 20th century, chocolate became even more popular with the rise of candy bars and other chocolate products. Today, the chocolate industry is worth billions of dollars, and people all over the world enjoy chocolate in many forms—from candy bars and cookies to hot chocolate and ice cream.

But chocolate also has a darker side. Most cacao is grown in developing countries, and many cacao farmers live in poverty. There are also concerns about child labor in some cacao-growing regions. And the environmental impact of cacao farming is a growing concern, as forests are cleared to make way for cacao plantations.

In recent years, there has been a growing movement for fair trade and sustainable chocolate, which aims to ensure that cacao farmers are paid fairly and that cacao is grown in an environmentally responsible way.
Despite these challenges, chocolate remains one of the most beloved foods in the world. And its long and fascinating history shows just how much this simple bean has shaped human culture and society.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Dreams have fascinated humans for thousands of years. People have always wondered what dreams mean, why we have them, and what they can tell us about ourselves. While we still don't have all the answers, modern science has taught us a lot about why we dream and what happens in our brains when we sleep.

First, let's talk about the stages of sleep. Sleep isn't just one thing—it's made up of several different stages that cycle throughout the night. One of these stages is called REM sleep, which stands for Rapid Eye Movement. REM sleep is the stage where most dreaming happens. During REM sleep, your brain is very active—almost as active as when you're awake—but your body is paralyzed, so you don't act out your dreams.

So why do we dream? There are many different theories. One of the most famous theories is Sigmund Freud's theory that dreams are a window into the unconscious mind, and that they represent our hidden desires, fears, and thoughts. Freud believed that dreams are a form of wish fulfillment, where we can act out things we can't do in real life. But most modern psychologists don't fully agree with Freud's theories anymore.

Another theory is the activation-synthesis theory, which suggests that dreams are just the brain's way of making sense of random neural activity that happens during sleep. According to this theory, dreams don't have any inherent meaning—they're just the brain trying to create a story out of random signals.

But more recent research suggests that dreams might actually serve important functions. One theory is that dreaming helps us process emotions and memories. During sleep, and especially during REM sleep, the brain processes and consolidates memories from the day, and dreams might be part of that process. Dreams can help us work through difficult emotions, process traumatic experiences, and integrate new information.

Another theory is that dreaming is a form of problem-solving. Some studies have found that people who sleep on a problem are better able to solve it the next day, and that dreams can help us think about problems in new and creative ways.

There's also evidence that dreams are important for mental health. People who are deprived of REM sleep often experience more anxiety, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. And people with certain mental health conditions, like depression and PTSD, often have more frequent and more intense nightmares.

While we still don't fully understand why we dream, what we do know is that dreaming is important. It's a normal and necessary part of sleep, and it plays a role in memory, emotion, and mental health. And even if we don't always remember our dreams, they're happening every night, helping our brains process and make sense of the world.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Public libraries are one of the most important institutions in modern society, yet they're often taken for granted. In an age where we can access almost any information online with just a few clicks, some people wonder if we still need libraries. But public libraries are more important than ever, and they offer much more than just books.

First and foremost, public libraries provide free and equal access to information and knowledge for everyone, regardless of income, education, or background. In a world where information is often behind paywalls and digital divides are real, libraries are places where anyone can walk in and access books, newspapers, magazines, databases, and the internet for free. This is especially important for low-income people, students, and anyone who can't afford to buy books or pay for internet access at home.

But libraries are much more than just collections of books. They're community centers that offer a wide range of services and programs. Many libraries offer free classes and workshops on everything from computer skills to job searching to creative writing. They have story time for children, book clubs for adults, and study spaces for students. Many libraries also offer free access to computers, printers, and Wi-Fi, which is essential for people who don't have these things at home.

Libraries also play an important role in promoting literacy and education. They help children develop a love of reading, they support students with their homework, and they provide resources for adult learners. In many communities, libraries are the only place where children and adults can access educational resources for free.

Another important function of libraries is that they provide safe, welcoming public spaces. Unlike cafes or bookstores, where you're expected to buy something, libraries are places where anyone can come and stay for as long as they want, no purchase necessary. They're places where people can read, study, work, or just relax. For homeless people and others who don't have a stable home, libraries can be a lifeline.

In recent years, libraries have been evolving to meet the changing needs of their communities. Many libraries now offer things like 3D printers, recording studios, and maker spaces. Some libraries lend out things like tools, seeds, and even museum passes. And many libraries offer social services, like help with housing, job training, and mental health resources.

Of course, libraries still have books—lots of them. And reading is still one of the most important things you can do for your education, your mental health, and your personal growth. But libraries are so much more than just books. They're essential community institutions that serve everyone, and they play a vital role in creating informed, educated, and connected communities.
